Abstract  
The paper discusses the policy implications of the Wirecard 
scandal. The study finds that all lines of defense against corporate 
fraud, including internal control systems, external audits, the 
oversight bodies for financial reporting and auditing and the 
market supervisor, contributed to the scandal and are in need of 
reform. To ensure market integrity and investor protection in the 
future, the authors make eight suggestions for the market and 
institutional oversight architecture in Germany and in Europe.

arguments.text: SRC-002 reports that a European Parliament ECON briefing says all five lines of defense failed in one way or another: Wirecard internal controls, supervisory board, external audit, financial reporting/audit oversight bodies, and BaFin. It says signals suggested fraudulent behavior years before revelation and identifies flawed market/institutional oversight as a root cause, while noting hindsight concerns. The briefing's preface says Wirecard had accounting inconsistency allegations from 2015, a 2016 Zatarra report accused it of money laundering and fraud; in January 2019 BaFin requested a FREP investigation after an FT report, restricted increases in net short positions for two months, and filed complaints against short sellers and the journalist. FT continued reporting alleged inflated sales/profits based on internal documents. KPMG was hired October 2019; its delayed April 2020 report said it could not verify €1bn in foreign bank accounts. BaFin filed a criminal complaint in June 2020 and days later Wirecard filed bankruptcy acknowledging €1.9bn in missing financial assets. SRC-001 is Wirecard's 28-Apr-2020 announcement: it said KPMG found no incriminating evidence of balance-sheet forgery and no significant findings requiring adjustment of 2016-2018 accounts, but said not all data needed to prove TPA revenues could be obtained because data were controlled by third parties; Wirecard said 200m+ December 2019 data were provided and no deviations were found, while KPMG identified documentation and organizational weaknesses. Treat Wirecard's statements as company assertions, not independently verified facts.
